agree.reason: The budget breakdown and the upfront admission of being a first-time creator would earn some trust, but a backer who has already lost $85 on a project that never shipped gets no delivery date, no refund promise and no update schedule, so they would likely hold back.

honest.reason: The numbers are accurate and the pitch avoids saying 'proven hit', but it says the convention players had never heard of the game without mentioning that most of the 23 ratings came from people at the creator's own table, and 'almost nothing else is left to go wrong' claims more than the facts support.

works_the_facts.reason: It correctly works out about 572 backers, about $5,150 for shipping, $2,800 in fees and about $2,650 left over, but it never compares the 572 backers needed with the 1,240 launch-email sign-ups (about 46% of them would need to back), which is the most persuasive figure available.

right_comparison.reason: The only contrast it offers is 'funding an idea' versus 'printing a finished game', which is a general claim; it does not compare against how first-time campaigns typically turn out or what the backer's real alternatives are.

qualification.reason: A risk-focused reader needs checkable commitments, and the pitch gives none: no November delivery date, no promise of an update every two weeks, and no full refund if delivery is more than three months late.

objections.reason: It deals with the first-time-creator concern and shows where the money goes, but it leaves out the main worry, which is whether the game will actually ship, and it skips the reviewer video, the refund and the delivery date, all of which answer that worry.

fit.reason: It is a pitch of about 480 words in a suitable form, but it still contains the placeholders [Game Title] and [Your name] even though the game is called Lantern Winter and the creator is Owen Hale.
